title: Justified by faith
hookLine: Protestants stress being declared right with God by faith in Christ

lines: A CHILDLESS MAN UNDER THE STARS.
HE BELIEVED, AND IT WAS COUNTED.
cards: Night, and a man with no children. In Genesis, God brings Abram outside and says: look up. "Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them."
So shall your descendants be. Abram has nothing to show for this promise. No baby, no plan, no proof.

Just the sky. Then comes the single sentence Paul will later build a whole argument on: "And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness." In this scene he does nothing but trust.

teach.b: To justify, in Paul's letters, is a courtroom word: a judge declaring someone in the right. Not making excuses for them. Pronouncing a verdict.
Day three hundred nine met this briefly; today, the courtroom itself.
Here's the startling line in Romans: God is the one "that justifieth the ungodly." Not the good. The ungodly.

And how? In Paul's words, "his faith is counted for righteousness," like Abram under the stars. So Paul writes, "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ."
The verdict comes first; peace follows. For the Protestant Reformers, this was the heart of it.
Martin Luther said he had been terrified of a God who judges, until he read Romans and saw that God's righteousness was something given, not demanded.
Their phrase was faith alone. Ephesians puts it plainly: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." Now the honest part.
James, in the same Bible, says: "Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only." Protestants read James as describing living faith, the kind that shows up in what you do.
Catholics teach that God's justifying grace both declares and truly makes a person righteous, with faith working through love, as Paul tells the Galatians.

Lutheran and Catholic leaders have signed a joint declaration sharing a basic understanding of justification, while still differing on details. Today's picture: a courtroom, and a verdict nobody earned.

how: Lutheran, Reformed and evangelical churches preach justification by grace through faith as the heart of the gospel, and Lutherans and some other Protestants mark Reformation Day each year; Catholic teaching speaks of justification as a gift of grace that also makes a person righteous.

o: giving good reasons to excuse what someone did wrong
God declaring a person in the right, received by faith
lining up text neatly along the edge of a page

p: it is the gift of God

s: in Romans, God justifies the good
Paul says God "justifieth the ungodly." the verdict is a gift.
James says a man is justified by works, and not by faith only
Protestants read it as living faith showing itself; Catholics read it with faith working through love.
Lutheran and Catholic leaders have never agreed on anything about justification
they have signed a joint declaration on a basic shared understanding, while still differing on details.

games.q: you're Abram. you have no children. God says, look at the stars: so shall your descendants be. what does Genesis say you do?
games.why: "and he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness." Paul builds his argument in Romans on this one line.

practice: Bring to mind something good in your life you didn't earn: a person who loves you, a morning, a second chance.
Notice the urge to explain why you deserve it, or to pay it back right away, and let it go quiet, the way Abram looked at the sky with nothing in his hands.
If you pray, thank God for it; if you don't, just say thank you, to no one in particular.

wordCard.voice: Justification. Being declared right with God, a verdict that Protestants stress is received by faith in Christ, as a gift.

orig.note: Greek: justification, a declaring right. Romans 4:25: raised again for our justification.

carryVoice: Your line: declared right. Abram had only the sky, and it was counted. Rest well.
